## Answers

**Question A** (L2, 64 B block → 8 words; $p_0=0.30$, $p_{i>0}=0.70/7=0.10$):

| Scheme | Average | Saving |
|---|---|---|
| (1) Neither | **160 CCs** = $90+7(10)$ | — |
| (2) Early restart only | **118 CCs** = $0.30(90)+0.10(910)$ | 26.25% |
| (3) Both | **110 CCs** (flat) | 31.25% |

Cases (1) and (3) don't depend on the distribution — in (1) you wait for the last word regardless, in (3) the requested word is always sent first. Only (2) is a genuine expectation.

**Question B** (L1, 32 B block → 4 words, uniform): back-solving $6/(x+12)=0.20$ gives blank 1 = **18 CCs**; then $(30-27)/30$ gives blank 2 = **10%**.

**Question C**: **more important for L2** — 31.25% vs 10% saving. The sharper point is that at L1 critical-word first *hurts*: its 9 CC surcharge exceeds the 6 CC early restart already saved, so 24 → 27 CCs, whereas at L2 it improves 118 → 110.

## Two things worth flagging

**An interpretation that Question B settles.** "With CWF it takes 110 CCs to get the first word" could mean a flat 110, or 110 only when CWF isn't a no-op. I took flat — and B independently confirms it: B demands *integer* blanks, and the flat reading gives exactly 10% while the alternative gives 17.5%. So B validates the assumption used in A.

**An environment bug not in `env.md`.** `\begin{itemize}` does not compile on this machine. The bullet needs a TS1 glyph, pdfTeX tries to generate bitmap font `tcrm1095`, and the write fails against read-only `~/.TinyTeX/texmf-var` — fatal, no PDF. I bisected it: `enumerate` and `description` are fine, `lmodern` fixes it. Covered both ways — my fragment uses no `itemize` (so it compiles under a bare CM preamble) *and* ships `lmodern` in `preamble.txt` to protect the master if another problem uses one. Worth propagating.

Verified beyond the maths: `lint_output.py` passes, the fragment compiles to a real PDF both with and without my preamble (0 errors, 0 undefined refs), and I read the rendered pages to check the tables and boxed answers. All numbers come from `solve.py` in exact rational arithmetic; `submission.md` maps each claim to its command.

Least confident: Question C is a judgement call, and I openly concede in it that miss *frequency* could tip the verdict toward L1 (break-even ≈16:1, which is reachable in real machines). I anchored the verdict to the per-miss reduction the problem actually computes rather than hiding the caveat.
